keyVerseText: Thus saith the LORD; Behold, I will give Pharaohhophra king of Egypt into the hand of his enemies, and into the hand of them that seek his life; as I gave Zedekiah king of Judah into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, his enemy, and that sought his life.
rootMeaning: The name פַּרְעֹה חׇפְרַע (Parʻôh Chophraʻ) is of Egyptian derivation, reflecting the historical and royal context of ancient Egypt. The Strong's definition highlights a compound sense: 'the great house - covering evil,' which suggests a royal title or name embodying authority and a protective yet possibly hidden or negative aspect. Although the root word is not specified, the etymology implies a complex identity tied to both majesty and moral ambiguity beyond the simple English title 'Pharaoh Hophra.'
usageInScripture: This term appears only once in Scripture, specifically in Jeremiah 44:30, where it refers to the Egyptian king reigning during Nebuchadnezzar's conquest. The top translation 'Pharaohhophra' is consistent and proper-name focused, emphasizing the historical figure rather than a generic title. This singular occurrence underscores the word's function as a precise identifier of a particular monarch rather than a broad term, revealing the specificity of biblical narrative in naming foreign rulers.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding פַּרְעֹה חׇפְרַע as a historical king with a name implying both grandeur and hidden evil enriches our grasp of biblical history and divine sovereignty. This name reminds believers that earthly rulers, even those with great power, operate under God’s ultimate authority and judgment. The connection to a king who opposed God's people during a critical period highlights the ongoing spiritual conflict between God's purposes and worldly powers. It calls Christians to trust in God's control over history and to recognize that all human authority is subject to His righteous will.
keyVerseReflection: Jeremiah 44:30 declares that the LORD will deliver Pharaohhophra, king of Egypt, into the hands of his enemies just as He did with Zedekiah of Judah. The use of this specific name emphasizes the certainty and historical reality of God's judgment on this ruler. It underscores that no king, regardless of their might or status, can escape God's sovereign plan. The word 'Pharaohhophra' here anchors the prophecy in a real historical context, reinforcing the trustworthiness of God's promises to His people.
